title: Build Your Game
tagline: Everything you have learned, in one game that is yours. This is the one you show people.
timing: Two periods works best: one to build, one to play-test and present.
newIdea: Restarting — and putting all nine lessons together
builtOn: Everything. Lessons 1 through 8, all at once.
goals: Combine everything you have learned into a complete, playable game with your character in it
Add a restart so the game can be played again without closing it
Make your own design decisions about difficulty, theme, rules, and how it ends
Go through the real cycle: build, test, adjust, test again

vocab.def: `draw()` running over and over is the engine of every game you have ever played
the rules that decide when the game ends, and how
resetting every variable and list back to its starting state so the game can be played again
actually playing your own game to find out whether it is fun, then changing it

warmup: Write one sentence describing your game. Who is your character? What are they collecting, and what are they avoiding? Two minutes, before any code.

howItWorks.h: You already know all of this
p: Look at the starter code below. There is exactly **one** thing in it you have not seen before. Everything else you have already built:
To restart a game, you might think you need to undo everything that happened. You do not. That is much harder and it never quite works.
Instead, you just **run the setup steps again**: make a new player, empty the lists and refill them, set the score back to 0, and set the flags back to false.

code.label: Reset by rebuilding

bullets: Notice that `setup()` now just calls `restartGame()`. Starting the game and restarting it are **the same thing**, so they should be the same code.
That is a genuinely important programming idea, and it is worth noticing that it made your code shorter, not longer.

p: Lesson 6 had two states: playing and game over. A real game usually has three — because winning and losing should not look the same.

code.label: Picking which screen to show

bullets: `&&` means **AND**. So `!gameOver && !playerWon` reads: "not lost, and not won" — in other words, still playing.

p: `mousePressed()` from Lesson 4 is an event function. Put the restart inside it, but guard it with an `if` so a click during play does not wipe your game.

code.label: Only restart when it is over

bullets: `||` means **OR**. "If we lost or we won, start over."

howItWorks.h: The starter code is a skeleton, not an answer
p: The plain colored blobs in the starter are **placeholders**. They are there so the code runs, not because they are what your game should look like.
Replace them with things that make sense in your world. That is not extra credit — that is the assignment.

steps: Write your one-sentence game description first. What is it about? Do this before touching code.
Start from your Lesson 8 sketch, or paste in the starter below — whichever is closer to what you want.
Run it and find each piece: `setup`, `draw`, `playGame`, `showWin`, `showGameOver`, `restartGame`, `mousePressed`. Say out loud what each one does.
Play it until you lose, then click to restart. Make sure that works before you change anything.
**Get one full loop working first.** Player, collectibles, and one win or lose condition. Do not add anything else until that plays properly.
Now replace the placeholders. Your character, your collectibles, your hazards, your world from Lesson 8.
Rewrite the win and lose screens in your own words. "YOU WIN!" is the starter's voice, not yours.
Tune the difficulty. Play it. Too easy? More hazards, or faster ones. Too hard? Fewer, or slower, or make your hitbox bigger.
Add one thing the lesson did not ask for. A second mechanic, an ability, lives, a level. Something that is your idea.
Play-test with a neighbor. Watch them play without helping them. Whatever confuses them is a real problem — go fix it.

code.label: Main sketch tab (builds on everything from Lessons 2–8)

makeItYours: **Theme it.** Replace every placeholder color, name, and shape with your world — space, ocean, forest, city, dream, whatever it is.
**Difficulty.** Make hazards faster over time. Add more when a wave is cleared. Give the player 3 lives instead of instant death.
**A second mechanic.** A `keyPressed()` special ability — a speed burst, a shield, a projectile, a teleport.
**Polish.** A title screen before the game starts. Better draw order. Animated decorations. A high score that survives a restart.
**A custom hazard.** Write a new `extends Blob` tab for an enemy that behaves differently — one that chases the player using `followMouse()`-style logic is genuinely scary.
challenge: Add a second level. When the player wins, instead of stopping, rebuild the world harder — more hazards, faster, a different background — and keep the score. That is `restartGame()` with a difficulty number, and it turns a demo into a game people want to keep playing.
flintHint: Good things to ask: "my restart is not resetting everything", "how do I add 3 lives?", "how do I make an enemy chase the player?", or "my game is too easy, what should I change?" Describe your game first so it can give you advice that fits.
wrapup: Play a neighbor's game. Tell them one thing you liked and one thing you would add.
assignmentTask: Build a complete, playable game starring your character. This is the capstone — the goal is a finished thing you are proud of, not a perfect one.
assignmentDo: Combine movement, control, lists, collisions, state, and your world into one game.
Write **both** a win condition and a lose condition. They should look different when they happen.
Make restart work, using `restartGame()` to reset by re-running your setup steps.
Replace every placeholder with something that belongs in your world.
Add at least one thing the lesson did not ask for — a rule, a mechanic, an ability that is your own idea.
Play-test it. Then change something because of what you learned. That last step is the one people skip.
submit: A screen recording of you playing your game, including winning **or** losing and then restarting.
Your answer to **Show your thinking** below.
checklist: Combine movement, control, lists, collisions, state, and world into one game.
Make and defend my own design decisions.
standard: Combine all prior skills into a complete, playable, replayable mini-game with win/lose conditions and independent design decisions.

stages.name: Getting Started
stages.text: The pieces are not coming together into something playable yet. **Next step:** get **one** full loop working first — player, collectibles, and a win or lose check — then build outward. Use `restartGame()` to reset by **re-running** your setup steps, not by undoing changes.

stages.name: Got It Working
stages.text: A playable game with my character: collectibles, a win and/or lose condition, a score, and a working restart.

stages.name: Made It Mine
stages.text: …and the game is unmistakably **mine** — themed world, my own rules and difficulty, my character at the center — with design decisions I made on purpose about how it plays.

stages.name: Went Beyond
stages.text: …and I pushed the game past the assignment in a direction **I** chose — a second mechanic that genuinely deepens play (lives, an ability, levels, a smart enemy), a rule nobody handed me, something I invented. The mark of this level is a design call that is mine, not cosmetics.

thinking: In two or three sentences: what is your game about? What design decision are you proudest of, and what would you add with another week?

di.h: Walk the structure — every piece should be familiar
p: Put the starter on the projector and name each function and where it came from. `setup()`, `draw()`, `playGame()`, `showWin()`, `showGameOver()`, `restartGame()`, `mousePressed()`.
The point of this walkthrough is confidence: they have written all of this before. There is exactly one new function today.
"To restart, we just run the same setup steps again — create a new player, clear the lists and fill them back up, reset score and gameOver to their starting values."
Point out that `setup()` is now just a call to `restartGame()`. Starting and restarting are the same operation, so they are the same code.

**This is the most important structural idea in the capstone**: reset state by re-running the initialization logic, not by trying to undo individual changes. It is a real software engineering principle and they can absolutely feel why it is better.

di.h: Three states and the new operators
p: `playerWon` joins `gameOver`, so `draw()` now picks between three screens.
`&&` (AND) and `||` (OR) show up here for the first time. Introduce them in plain language when you hit them, not as a separate topic: "not lost AND not won means still playing."

di.h: Say plainly that the starter is a skeleton
p: Emphasise this hard: **students SHOULD change everything.** The blob obstacles are placeholders. Replacing them with something that makes sense in their world is the assignment, not a bonus.
Some students will treat the starter as sacred and only change colors. Head that off in the first five minutes.
Tell them explicitly: get **one full loop** working first — player, collectibles, one end condition — and only then build outward.
The students who struggle in this capstone are almost always the ones who tried to add five features before the first one played correctly.

guided: Two minutes of writing: a one-sentence game description. Do this before any code. Students who can say what their game is build much better games.
Run the starter together and identify each piece out loud.
Play until you lose, then click to restart, as a class. Confirm the loop works before anyone changes anything.
Everyone replaces the placeholder collectible with something themed. One quick win, immediately.
Release to build. Circulate constantly. The main intervention you will make all period is "get one thing working before you add the next thing."
**Mid-way, stop everyone for five minutes of play-testing with a neighbor.** Watching someone else play your game without helping them is the fastest way to find out what is broken.
Final period: demo day. Every student plays a neighbor's game and names one thing they would add.
pitfalls: **Adding features before the core loop works.** The number one cause of a frustrated capstone. Intervene early and often.
**`restartGame()` that misses a variable** — score resets but hazards do not, or the player stays dead. Have them check every global against the reset function, one at a time.
**Rebuilding `ground` inside `restartGame()`** is fine, but rebuilding it inside `draw()` is not. Watch for creation code drifting into the wrong function.
Hazards looped **backwards** unnecessarily — harmless, but a sign they are copying rather than choosing.
**`keyboardControl()` coasting**: velocity stays set after key release, so the player drifts. If they want it to stop, `keyReleased()` with `setVelocity(0, 0)`. Fine to introduce if they ask.
Difficulty tuned by the person who built it, who is therefore excellent at it. Almost every student game is too hard. Play-testing with a neighbor fixes this.
teacher.wrapupAnswer: For the final share-out you want each student to be able to name their game in a sentence and point at one decision they made on purpose. That is the real evidence of the capstone.
notes: **The goal is ownership and completion, not polish or correctness.** A finished janky game beats an unfinished elegant one, every time.
**Consider splitting into two periods:** period 1 to build, period 2 to play-test and present. The presentation is not optional filler — an audience changes how much students care.
Students who finish early should be pushed toward a **second mechanic** (lives, a power-up, a level 2), not more cosmetics. The extra complexity is where the real learning is.
The `restartGame()` pattern is the structural takeaway. If a student remembers one thing from this lesson in a year, that is the one worth remembering.

Bonus Lesson C (Animation) drops in beautifully here — students often want their character to feel alive rather than sliding around as one frozen drawing. Note that an `AnimatedSprite` is not a `Blob`, so it uses `distanceTo()` instead of `collidesWith()`.
Bonus Lessons A (Images) and B (Sounds) also land well during this capstone for students who want polish.
Watch for students who will not change the starter. Sit with them and ask what their game is *about* — usually they have an idea and did not realize they were allowed to build it.
